text:
Emily Scolnick is a 2026 Dow Jones News Fund intern at the Pennsylvania Capital-Star.

Pennsylvania’s Solar for Schools program has been renewed for a third year, receiving $25 million in this year’s state budget to help schools utilize solar energy and cut costs.

State Rep. Elizabeth Fielder (D-Philadelphia), who chairs the House Energy Committee, first introduced the program in 2024. It provides grants through the state Department of Community and Economic Development to lower the price of installing solar energy systems at schools across the state.

“Our schools are not exempt from the affordability crisis facing Pennsylvania,” Fielder wrote in a release. “My hope is that Solar for Schools offers a tool to help them combat rising, unpredictable energy costs and put the money toward what matters most: educating our young people.”

Grants can now cover up to 75% of the total cost of a solar project, up from the previous maximum of 50%. Districts can also enter power-purchase agreements with solar developers to more easily arrange for panel installation and secure lower, fixed energy rates, according to the release.

A spokesperson for Fielder said the option for agreements aims to help schools manage the upfront costs that come with owning solar panels.

Representatives from the Pennsylvania Building and Construction Trades Council and the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers applauded the state’s decision to maintain funding for the program.

“The highly skilled men and women of the IBEW are proud to be a key part of these solar installations across the state,” IBEW representative Kris Anderson said. “In addition to jobs for our members, Solar for Schools creates tremendous opportunities to save schools money and create hands-on training opportunities for the next generation of workers.”

The program contributes to Pennsylvania’s transition to renewable energy, while creating jobs, adds more sources to combat the higher demand for energy from data centers, and helps students understand the benefits of solar energy.

It would also save schools around $342 million during the lifetime of the systems, according to estimates from PennEnvironment.

The Trump administration has rolled back federal programs promoting clean energy, especially since the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last summer, forcing states to take greater ownership of their renewable energy programs.

School districts, charter schools, cyber charter schools, community colleges, and other educational entities are all eligible for grants from the Solar for Schools program.

Seventy-three schools and districts across 23 counties received funding during the first year of the program, and applications for new funding are accepted on a rolling basis.

The Community College of Philadelphia, Bloomsburg Area School District, and Exeter School District are among those expected to break ground on solar panel construction by the end of this year.

New report: New EDF and Gridworks research highlights the value of intervenor compensation.

Key finding: Bringing more voices to the table can lead to more informed and durable energy decisions.

Recommendations: The report offers practical guidance for states designing or strengthening intervenor compensation programs.

Environmental Defense Fund, a science-based environmental nonprofit, and Gridworks today released Powering Participation: How Intervenor Compensation Can Strengthen Utility Commission Decision-Making, a new report examining how intervenor compensation programs can help state utility commissions make more informed, durable decisions as they navigate rapid changes across the energy system.

"Utility commissions are making some of the most consequential energy decisions in decades," said Jolette Westbrook, Director & Senior Attorney, Regulatory Solutions at Environmental Defense Fund. "Strong decisions depend on strong evidentiary records. Intervenor compensation helps ensure commissions hear the full range of expertise and perspectives needed to test assumptions, strengthen analysis and better serve the public."

As electricity demand grows, utility commissions are making increasingly complex decisions about affordability, reliability, transmission planning and grid modernization. The report finds that well-designed intervenor compensation programs – which help public interest organizations, consumer advocates, Tribes and community-based organizations participate in utility commission proceedings by generally covering the costs of their time as well as legal, technical and expert support – can strengthen the evidentiary record by ensuring commissioners hear from a broader range of expertise, independent analysis and stakeholder perspectives. The report identifies practical recommendations to help states establish or strengthen these programs.

"As more states consider creating or expanding intervenor compensation programs, the details matter," said Janea A. Scott, Senior Fellow at Gridworks. "This report examines what's working across the country, where programs continue to face challenges and how thoughtful design can improve both public participation and regulatory decision-making."

Drawing on original research, surveys, interviews with more than 64 regulators and advocates, and case studies from across the country, the report shows how effective intervenor compensation programs represent a targeted, cost-effective investment that can help commissions identify risks earlier, evaluate alternatives and improve long-term outcomes for customers and communities.

The report identifies several best practices, including clear eligibility standards, funding structures that reduce barriers to participation, transparent program administration and technical assistance that helps new participants engage effectively. It also highlights six state case studies that illustrate different approaches and lessons learned.

The report concludes that funding alone is not enough. Outreach, technical assistance and clear procedural guidance are also essential to help communities and public interest organizations participate meaningfully in complex utility commission proceedings. It also recognizes that intervenor compensation is just one tool for supporting public participation. In some cases, workshops, informational meetings and other informal opportunities for dialogue may be more appropriate.

India EV Retail Sales Reach Historic Record in June 2026

India's electric vehicle industry achieved one of its biggest milestones in June 2026 as retail EV sales crossed an impressive 306,220 units, making it one of the strongest months in the country's EV history. The achievement becomes even more significant because electric passenger vehicle sales reached 31,823 units, while overall EV penetration exceeded 12% for the very first time.

This milestone highlights India's rapid transition toward sustainable transportation and demonstrates how government policies, expanding charging infrastructure, improving battery technology, and increasing consumer awareness are transforming the automotive industry.

A Historic Month for India's EV Industry

The Indian electric vehicle market has been growing consistently over the past few years, but June 2026 marks a turning point. Crossing more than 306,000 retail sales indicates that EV adoption is no longer limited to early adopters—it is becoming mainstream.

Industry analysts believe this growth reflects increasing customer confidence, wider product availability, and better financing options.

Passenger Electric Vehicles Continue Strong Growth

One of the biggest highlights was the performance of passenger electric vehicles. Sales reached 31,823 units, showing that Indian consumers are increasingly willing to switch from traditional petrol and diesel vehicles to electric mobility.

Affordable pricing, lower running costs, government incentives, and expanding charging infrastructure have significantly improved consumer confidence.

EV Penetration Crosses 12%

Perhaps the most important achievement is that EV penetration crossed the 12% mark for the first time. This means that more than one out of every ten vehicles sold in India is now electric.

Only a few years ago, EV penetration remained below 2%, making this growth remarkable.

Government Policies Driving Growth

Several government initiatives have played a crucial role in accelerating EV adoption:

State-level EV incentives

Tax benefits for buyers

Expansion of charging stations

Production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes

Battery manufacturing incentives

Support for domestic EV manufacturing

These policies have encouraged both manufacturers and consumers to embrace electric mobility.

Charging Infrastructure Expansion

Charging infrastructure has improved significantly across metropolitan cities and highways. Public charging stations continue to expand, reducing range anxiety among consumers.

Fast charging technology is also becoming increasingly common, making long-distance EV travel more practical.

Battery Technology Improvements

Lower battery costs are also helping reduce vehicle prices.

Indian Automakers Accelerating EV Production

Domestic manufacturers are rapidly expanding their EV portfolios. New launches across passenger cars, SUVs, two-wheelers, and commercial vehicles are providing consumers with more choices than ever before.

International manufacturers are also investing heavily in India's growing EV ecosystem.

Consumer Awareness at an All-Time High

Consumers today understand the long-term financial benefits of electric vehicles. Lower fuel costs, reduced maintenance expenses, and environmental advantages are influencing purchase decisions.

Fleet Electrification

Ride-sharing companies, logistics operators, and commercial fleets are rapidly electrifying their vehicles. Fleet demand is becoming a major contributor to EV sales.

Economic Benefits

Growing EV adoption creates thousands of jobs in manufacturing, battery production, charging infrastructure, software development, and maintenance services.

India is also positioning itself as a global hub for EV manufacturing and battery production.

Environmental Impact

Higher EV adoption contributes to lower greenhouse gas emissions and improved urban air quality. As renewable energy generation increases, electric vehicles become even cleaner throughout their lifecycle.

Challenges Remaining

Battery raw material availability

Charging infrastructure in rural regions

High upfront vehicle prices

Grid modernization

Addressing these challenges will ensure sustainable long-term growth.

Future Outlook

Industry experts expect India's EV market to continue growing rapidly over the coming decade. Increasing affordability, domestic battery manufacturing, technological innovation, and supportive government policies are likely to push EV penetration well beyond current levels.

The country is also expected to become one of the world's largest electric vehicle markets by the end of the decade.

June 2026 represents a landmark moment for India's electric vehicle industry. Crossing 306,220 EV retail sales and achieving more than 12% market penetration demonstrates that electric mobility has entered the mainstream.

With improving infrastructure, innovative vehicle launches, supportive policies, and growing consumer confidence, India is firmly positioned to become a global leader in sustainable transportation.

text:
California’s Central Valley is one of the country’s richest farming regions, blessed with fertile soils, sunny days and a massive man-made system of irrigation canals and reservoirs.

But as climate change intensifies, droughts deepen, and water restrictions kick in, growers in much of the valley are getting less water for their fields. They also face new limits on how much they can pump from underground, forcing them to leave hundreds of thousands of acres dry in the coming years. Some are turning to an answer they never thought they’d embrace: solar.

“We still want to farm, but taking the chance that water will be here was too risky,” said Todd Tracy, a fifth-generation farmer, as he drove through his groves of green pistachio trees about a half-hour west of Bakersfield.

In 2021, he optioned about a third of his family’s 8,600 acres to a solar developer, Avantus. The company is planning the largest solar-plus-storage project in the country, called Buttonbush. Its panels will eventually cover almost 12,000 acres and link up to a substation near the tiny town of Buttonwillow, before sending two gigawatts of electricity, enough to power 1 million homes, across the state.

“We weren’t all for this, but we had to find a use for this ground,” Tracy said of the discussions among his family members when they were first approached by the developer.

The farm grows cotton, corn, wheat, carrots, potatoes, pistachios and almonds. But stretching between the planted fields lie wide swaths of dusty, brown soil, fields fallowed over the years for lack of water. The home Tracy’s father lived in before he died in 2024 sits in a cluster of trees right next to one.

“We’re still paying mortgages, we’re still paying taxes and employees, and we see the writing on the wall,” Tracy said.

What the writing says is dire. Roughly half the farm receives water from Northern California via a vast system of aqueducts. The amount has been shrinking for two decades, and this year growers got 45% of what they are allotted.

The rest of the fields rely on water pumped from underground, and that’s also getting squeezed as California’s Sustainable Groundwater Management Act kicks in. Tracy says growers in his area could see 30% cuts by 2040.

The law was adopted in 2014 to address acute overpumping causing dry wells and sinking ground. Pumping limits ratchet down each year until 2040 in many areas, and farmers now face fines if they exceed them.

“I want to be optimistic, but being realistic, there’s not going to be water there in 2040,” Tracy said, pointing to a 600-acre field of “very good soil” left bare since he ripped out almonds at the end of their 25-year productive cycle two years ago.

He said he may need to lay off five or six seasonal workers once all the land in the solar project moves out of production.

Kern County approved Buttonbush solar in March. It includes land from about 18 farmers in the Semitropic Water District and neighboring Rosedale-Rio Bravo Water Storage District.

“Now we’re just waiting for the developer to move,” Tracy’s cousin Mike Frey said. “It’s looking like they will.”

Buttonbush is one of dozens of large, 100-plus megawatt solar fields cropping up across water-stressed regions of the state, especially the San Joaquin Valley.

Researchers at the Public Policy Institute of California estimate as much as 20% of the valley’s irrigated land may go dry by 2040.

“Growers are feeling pinched,” Caitlin Peterson, associate director of the PPIC Water Policy Center, said. “Solar is one of the potential options for folks that are having to take land out of production that has the potential to be fairly lucrative.”

Farmers’ desperation coincides with California’s solar dreams. The state is legally mandated to reach 100% clean electricity by 2045. That will require an additional 10 gigawatts of clean energy a year and between 0.5 and 1.3 million acres of in-state solar development, the California Energy Commission says.

Solar on retired farmland in the Central Valley could go a long way, potentially 30 gigawatts of the way, according to the PPIC, toward meeting that goal.

Some of the largest arrays are planned for places that have historically been bastions of anti-solar sentiment.

Just three years ago, several board members of the Westlands Water District, the largest agricultural water agency in the Central Valley, expressed concern about solar. “I thought we were a farming board,” one said when the prospect of converting more land came up.

Since then, the Westlands Solar Park, which launched in 2016 as a small pilot, has continued to expand toward a 2.27-gigawatt target in Kings and Fresno counties. The 1.15-gigawatt Darden Clean Energy Project broke ground this year in Fresno, also in Westlands.

But the biggest indication of the shift came in December, when the Westlands board of directors approved converting 135,000 acres, about a fifth of all the land in the irrigation district, into a giant network of solar farms.

More than half that land is owned by the district but is unsuitable for farming. The ground is loaded with crop-harming salts, or in some areas prone to sinking if pumping resumes.

Individual growers will also put land into the project.

A decade ago, converting farmland to solar farms was “something nobody wanted to talk about,” Allison Febbo, Westlands’ general manager, said. But now, “I kind of call it our survival plan into the future.”

Advocates say retired farmlands are some of the best places for solar because permitting is faster than on ecologically sensitive desert areas. Unlike farmland converted to housing, solar installations could more easily revert back to farming at the end of a project’s 30-year lifespan.

And, according to a recent report from the Solar Energy Industries Assn., there is more than enough fallowed land in California to meet the solar need.

But not all farmers want solar. A 1965 law, the Williamson Act, was designed to preserve farmland from suburban sprawl by giving tax breaks to growers if they agree to keep their land in farming.

There’s a hefty fee for breaking a contract, which the solar industry has been trying to get rid of for years, most recently with a proposed bill from Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland). Some farming groups consistently fight the effort.

“Water availability in California changes all the time, and the response has never been to give people a free pass out of a contract they signed,” said Peter Ansel, director of policy at the California Farm Bureau. He said the organization would want to see any changes to existing law tailored narrowly to only the most water-stressed areas and not allow full cancellation with no fees.

Yet in a sign of the changing times, the Kern County Farm Bureau broke last year with the state Farm Bureau on this to support Wicks’ bill after hearing from members who wanted solar.

“Kern would prefer to have water and to have farmland being farmland,” said Todd Snider, president of the Kern County Farm Bureau. “If that’s not an option, we advocate for property right holders to do what they want to do with their property.”

Westlands Water District is pushing the state grid operator to prioritize more transmission lines in the Central Valley, Febbo said. If that happens, construction of one of the world’s biggest solar complexes could start within five years.

title: Battery electric vehicle prices fell 18% and model choice quadrupled between 2020 and 2025
description:
Battery prices have fallen – savings not yet fully passed on Global battery prices fell by 21%–24% in nominal terms between 2020 and 2025 – from around €165–€185 per kilowatt-hour to about €130–€140.
So far, the lower battery prices have had only a limited impact on vehicle prices.
Model diversity is growing; room for improvement in the small car segment The number of available battery electric models rose from 38 in 2020 to 159 in 2025.
The range of internal combustion engine models declined from 275 to 194 over the same period.
A disparity persists in the mini and small car segment: in 2025, there were 19 electric models compared to 35 internal combustion engine models.
text:
“Our results show that the market for electric cars has evolved significantly in recent years. Today, these vehicles offer, on average, longer ranges and more engine power, while the actual prices of comparable models have fallen. This a clear indicator of where Europe’s automotive market is headed,” said Peter Mock, Europe Managing Director at the ICCT.

Average prices rise due to a changing vehicle mix – models themselves are becoming more affordable

In Germany, the average list price for electric vehicles rose nominally from around €37,000 to about €53,000 between 2020 and 2025. However, this increase does not reflect higher prices for comparable vehicles, but rather a shift in the model lineup: The share of mid-range and upper-mid-range vehicles in the electric vehicle lineup rose significantly from 2020 to 2025 and now accounts for 73% of all electric models. However, when individual models are tracked over time and vehicle characteristics such as weight, engine power, and range – as well as inflation – are taken into account, the prices of comparable electric vehicles fell by around 18% over the same period. Real prices for vehicles with internal combustion engines, on the other hand, rose by around 2% over the same period.

Battery prices have fallen – savings not yet fully passed on

Global battery prices fell by 21%–24% in nominal terms between 2020 and 2025 – from around €165–€185 per kilowatt-hour to about €130–€140. Adjusted for inflation, this corresponds to a price reduction of about 35%–37%. So far, the lower battery prices have had only a limited impact on vehicle prices. However, the average electric range increased by about one-third during the study period, suggesting that savings were invested in vehicle improvements or on recouping research and development costs.

“The significant drop in battery costs has not yet fully translated into lower list prices. This means that the potential for further price reductions in electric vehicles has not yet been exhausted,” Prof. Dr. Patrick Plötz, Head of the Department of Energy Technology and Energy Systems at Fraunhofer ISI and one of the study’s authors.

Model diversity is growing; room for improvement in the small car segment

The number of available battery electric models rose from 38 in 2020 to 159 in 2025. The range of internal combustion engine models declined from 275 to 194 over the same period.

“The number of electric models has grown fourfold in just five years. In the medium and upper medium segments, meaning mid-size and larger cars, consumers now have roughly as many electric options as combustion engine vehicles,” explains Kyle Morrison, ICCT researcher and co-author of the study. A disparity persists in the mini and small car segment: in 2025, there were 19 electric models compared to 35 internal combustion engine models.

6:00

Energy

Michigan Data Centers: The Weekly Download

News and updates on data centers in the Great Lakes State for the week of July 13

States Newsroom graphic illustration

New Developments

Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer unveiled her Michigan Affordable and Responsible Growth Action Plan, intended to ensure data centers don’t bring harm to Michigan residents. Her approach is two-pronged, calling on state lawmakers to pass protections for Michigan energy customers, while asking data center companies to commit to paying their own way, and abiding by energy and environmental regulations. As of Thursday afternoon, the Governor had secured commitments from six companies.

The Wixom City Council unanimously rejected a request to waive its data center moratorium for developers eyeing a 54-acre spot on Wixom Road, MLive’s Peg McNichol reports. The moratorium remains in effect until the end of August.

Lansing City Council has approved a 182-day moratorium on data center developments, blocking considerations of new proposals until Jan. 25, 2027, Emma J. Nelson reports for WKAR.

Updates

The Saline Township Board of Trustees approved the full amount of a tax break requested for the controversial data center under development in their community, backtracking on a decision to approve a significantly smaller tax break earlier in the week, MLive’s Jennifer Eberbach reports. Oracle America Cloud Services LLC requested a 50% reduction in property taxes for 12 years. While the board previously capped the valuation of the project at $4.8 billion, it would later remove the cap on advice from one of the township attorneys, approving the tax break at the the project’s current valuation of $43 billion.

Ingham County Clerk Barb Byrum has approved recall petitions for Mason Councilwoman Elaine Ferris, according to WLNS’s Trevor King. The recall effort was prompted by residents’ opposition to a data center proposed in the community.

Developers of the proposed Project Flex data center in Lyon Township are continuing to push forward, with WXYZ’s Christiana Ford reporting that the township’s planning commission is expected to review the project at its meeting on Monday, Aug. 24.

News of Note

Lucas Smolcic Larson and Danielle James of MLive report that between 2020 and 2024 data centers benefitted from $13 million in tax breaks that the Legislature approved in 2015.

On Tuesday the Huron Valley Area Labor Federation issued a statement calling for a pause on approving large-scale data center projects until safeguards are put in place. The group of 40 labor unions specified that in order for a project to move forward, eight minimum standards must be met.

Those standards include no tax incentives or subsidies, no cost shifting onto consumers, binding labor standards, full transparency and public disclosure, enforceable limits on resource use, no weakening of state climate commitments, safeguards for community protections and accountability and democratic review, approval, and oversight of these projects.

CNBC’s Justin Papp examines the role AI and data center concerns could play headed into Michigan’s Aug. 4 U.S. Senate Primary.

description:
The investment was made by the IIA in colaboration with the Energy and Infrastructure Ministry in a push to "promote a new generation of Israeli innovations in renewable energy technologies for the marine environment," the statement by the IIA said.
The objective is to invest in projects focused on offshore renewable energy generation and artificial intelligence-powered marine energy management systems.
Perfect development ecosystem According to the IIA, the project will fund applied research that advances the sustainable development of Israel's marine environment while enabling the development and commercialization of innovative Blue-Tech Energy technologies as part of Israel's broader energy and climate objectives.
"We are working to harness our marine resources to develop green, clean energy solutions that will strengthen our energy security and expand the use of renewable energy," said Energy and Infrastructure Minister Eli Cohen.
"We receive true treasures from the sea, and now we are giving back through marine research and the development of innovative technologies.
text:
The Israel Innovation Authority (IIA) announced on Sunday a new fund to support research and development of marine-focused energy solutions, with an initial NIS 6 million invested in what the IIA calls "Blue-Tech Energies."

The investment was made by the IIA in colaboration with the Energy and Infrastructure Ministry in a push to "promote a new generation of Israeli innovations in renewable energy technologies for the marine environment," the statement by the IIA said.

The objective is to invest in projects focused on offshore renewable energy generation and artificial intelligence-powered marine energy management systems.

The initiative consists of NIS 6 million in investments, NIS 3 million of which will be drawn from the Israel Citizens Fund of the Energy Ministry.

"Israel benefits from a unique combination of scientific excellence, entrepreneurship, and a world-class technology industry, and this new call for proposals is designed to harness those strengths to develop a new generation of marine energy technologies," said Dror Bin, CEO of the Israel Innovation Authority.

"Through our collaboration with the Energy and Infrastructure Ministry, we seek to transform high-quality research into applied innovation, strengthen collaboration between academia and industry, and reinforce Israel's position as one of the world's leading nations in the development of advanced energy solutions," he added.

Perfect development ecosystem

According to the IIA, the project will fund applied research that advances the sustainable development of Israel's marine environment while enabling the development and commercialization of innovative Blue-Tech Energy technologies as part of Israel's broader energy and climate objectives.

"We are working to harness our marine resources to develop green, clean energy solutions that will strengthen our energy security and expand the use of renewable energy," said Energy and Infrastructure Minister Eli Cohen.

"We will continue investing in groundbreaking Israeli innovation and increasing clean energy production for the benefit of the health of Israel's citizens and to reinforce the country's energy security," he added.

The program will be available to any company or research center developing technologies in this sector, with another key objective of improving collaboration among academia, industry, and the government.

"We receive true treasures from the sea, and now we are giving back through marine research and the development of innovative technologies. I am grateful for the opportunity to contribute to the people of Israel," said MK Nissim Vaturi (Likud), Chairman of the Committee for Oversight of the Israeli Citizens' Fund.

title: Moeve Chemicals achieves full global verification for production of Low Carbon solutions
description:
Moeve Chemicals has completed the verification of its global manufacturing network for the production of Low Carbon products.
The verification process, carried out by AENOR (the Spanish Association for Standardization and Certification), is supported by Moeve Chemicals' proprietary in-house verification system.
This approach provides customers with confidence in the environmental claims associated with Low Carbon products.
"Reaching full verification across our global manufacturing network is a major milestone for Moeve Chemicals," said Alfredo López Carretero, Global Head of Safety, Energy & Sustainability at Moeve Chemicals .
"It demonstrates our ability to offer Low Carbon solutions consistently across all our production sites and allows us to support customers around the world with verified, traceable products that contribute to their decarbonization goals."
text:
Moeve Chemicals has completed the verification of its global manufacturing network for the production of Low Carbon products. Following the latest verification milestone at its Brazil and Shanghai facilities, all of the company's production plants are now enabled to manufacture and supply products within its Low Carbon portfolio, strengthening Moeve Chemicals' ability to support customers worldwide in their decarbonization journeys.

Designed to help customers reduce the carbon footprint of their products while maintaining the same quality, performance and reliability standards associated with conventional alternatives, the Low Carbon portfolio reflects Moeve Chemicals’ commitment to advancing more sustainable chemical solutions and supporting emissions reductions across customers’ value chains.

Among the products included in the portfolio are NextLab Low Carbon, the lower-carbon version of linear alkylbenzene (LAB), a key raw material used in the production of biodegradable detergents, and NextPhenol Low Carbon, a lower-carbon alternative for phenol and its derivatives, widely used in applications ranging from resins and adhesives to automotive and construction materials. The global availability of these solutions enables customers across diverse industries to advance their decarbonization objectives without compromising product performance or quality.

The verification process, carried out by AENOR (the Spanish Association for Standardization and Certification), is supported by Moeve Chemicals' proprietary in-house verification system. This system was developed to ensure transparency, traceability and consistency in the allocation and management of renewable energy attributes used across its operations. This approach provides customers with confidence in the environmental claims associated with Low Carbon products.

"Reaching full verification across our global manufacturing network is a major milestone for Moeve Chemicals," said Alfredo López Carretero, Global Head of Safety, Energy & Sustainability at Moeve Chemicals ."It demonstrates our ability to offer Low Carbon solutions consistently across all our production sites and allows us to support customers around the world with verified, traceable products that contribute to their decarbonization goals."

The completion of this process further strengthens Moeve Chemicals' position as a leading global supplier of chemical products and represents another step forward in delivering innovative solutions that help customers advance their sustainability objectives while maintaining the highest standards of performance and quality.

text:
The oil and electric industries are rallying around Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, helping him rake in more than $25 million over four months and boosting other statewide Republican candidates.

Democrats, whose fundraising trails the GOP in most statewide races, said they’ve raised enough money to stay in the fight — while arguing that the gusher of oil money shows their opponents are out of touch.

Texas gasoline prices sit well below the national average, but on Sunday, the state average was about 29 percent higher than a year earlier, according to AAA. And Texas’ data center construction boom has rural residents worried about the impact on their local electric rates, as well as the disruption of living near new facilities and the power plants they require.

Advertisement

Those issues are in play as Abbott seeks a fourth consecutive term as governor. He’ll have to beat Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa in November.

“Follow Greg Abbott’s money and you’ll find everything wrong with government,” said Hinojosa campaign spokesperson Tommy Kubitschek in a statement.

Eduardo Leal, a spokesperson for Abbott’s campaign, said in an email that the governor “continues to earn broad support from Texans because of his proven record of slashing property taxes, securing the border, and keeping Texas affordable.” Leal said contributions to Abbott’s campaign are publicly disclosed and in keeping with Texas law.

Big money is nothing new in Texas politics, where there’s no limit on individual campaign contributions in most statewide races. In the 2022 governor’s race, Abbott and Democratic challenger Beto O’Rourke raised and spent about $160 million combined.

Abbott has argued that the Texas economy, which is generally faring better than the national economy, shows his approach is working. Still, government watchdog groups have said for years that the growing cost of Texas campaigns is damaging trust in politics.

“The result is that a few individuals with wealth unimaginable to working Texans can buy the type of government they want, rather than the one the people might otherwise choose,” Adrian Shelley, Texas director of Public Citizen, said in a statement.

But sometimes the energy industry has to adjust to voters.

That happened in this year’s Republican primary runoff for a spot on the state Railroad Commission, which regulates oil and gas operations in Texas. Challenger Bo French toppled incumbent Jim Wright, despite notable oil and gas support for Wright. French is now aiming to defeat Democratic state Rep. Jon Rosenthal and keep the commission seat in GOP hands.

In the governor’s race, Abbott started the year with $106 million in his campaign fund, and after spending for the March primary election — and raking in $25.5 million in the latest cycle — had $67.2 million to spend on the general election, according to his latest filing.

Hinojosa raised $6.2 million over the last four months and reported about $3 million in cash available as of last week, her filing showed. Her campaign said she relied heavily on small donors.

In the most recent campaign season, Abbott picked up donations from political action committees run by the Texas Oil and Gas Association and Chevron, along with individual contributions from oil executives. That included Javaid Anwar ($1.25 million) and Double Eagle co-founders Cody Campbell ($300,000) and John Sellers ($250,000).

Musk money

And donations from big names aren’t limited to the oil business. Tesla CEO Elon Musk donated $500,000 to both Abbott’s campaign and Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick’s campaign.

A PAC associated with Oncor Electric Delivery — the state-regulated company that provides the electric distribution network for much of northern Texas — gave Abbott’s campaign $100,000. Oncor CEO Allen Nye contributed $170,000 and six other Oncor executives kicked in a combined $95,000.

Oncor’s Nye also donated $150,000 to Patrick’s campaign and gave $20,000 to Mayes Middleton, the Republican running for Texas attorney general, records show.

Oncor said the company was advocating for its interests, although the donations came from company employees.

“Political contributions are funded by an Oncor employee group, not rate payers, and are not based on party lines or individual issues,” Oncor spokesperson Kerri Dunn said in an email. “Personal donations from leadership are similarly not funded by rate payers nor based on party lines or individual issues.”

None of Abbott’s other major energy donors responded to requests for comments.

Patrick’s campaign benefited from many of the same donors as Abbott, including Musk and Oncor’s Nye.

The lieutenant governor raised $5 million during the latest period and has $35 million in his campaign account. His opponent, state Rep. Vikki Goodwin, raised $397,000 during the same time and had $317,000 on hand.

Goodwin said people are willing to give Democrats a chance, even in conservative rural areas, because of both President Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the impact of Texas Republican policies.

“Particularly with the data center issue right now, people are very worried about their water and energy prices increasing,” she said in an interview.

Democrats have their own reliable funding sources, although they tend to give an order of magnitude less than Republican donors.

State Rep. James Talarico, the Democrat running for U.S. Senate who has become a prolific fundraiser as he battles Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in the race, has donated $100,000 to Hinojosa’s campaign and either given or promised contributions to other statewide Democrats this cycle.

Annie’s List, an Austin-based organization that promotes progressive women candidates, gave $10,000 to Hinojosa’s campaign this cycle, records show, and the Texas American Federation of Teachers contributed $75,000.

Don Henley, the frontman for the Eagles rock band who grew up in East Texas, gave $109,000 to Goodwin’s campaign along with smaller donations to other candidates.

Henley was unavailable for comment, according to his publicist, and the other major Democratic donors didn’t respond to emails seeking comment.

At least two of the Republican candidates are self-funding part of their campaigns with family money. Middleton, an heir to an oil and gas fortune, loaned $15.2 million to his own campaign during the Republican primary for attorney general, according to Transparency USA.

Texas state Sen. Nathan Johnson, who’s running against Middleton, said in an interview that Middleton has essentially unlimited money and that he’s counting on voters being disenchanted with Republicans in general and with the individual candidates.

Middleton, for instance, branded himself “MAGA Mayes” in the primary election, which may not help in the general election.

Likewise, the Republican nominee for state comptroller, Don Huffines, comes from a wealthy family and has largely self-funded his own campaign. He is also serving as comptroller for the rest of this year after being tapped for that role by Abbott.

Sarah Eckhardt, a state senator who’s running against Huffines, said Democrats are working together to overcome the funding gap, often scheduled campaign stops together.

Eckhardt had $240,000 in her campaign account as of last week, compared to $1.1 million for Huffines. She said that’s enough to mount a competitive race.

“It’s not going to be a multimillion dollar campaign, but we don’t need multimillions,” she said. “We need votes.”

title: New government can revitalise North Sea energy industry with policy reset
description:
Energy policy cannot be made in Westminster alone.
The new government has an opportunity to reset the relationship with the North Sea industry and the communities that depend on it.
Using imported liquified natural gas (LNG) from America or Qatar which is increasingly being used to replace North Sea gas, involves carbon emissions that are four times higher.
Government policy should back North Sea production as part of a secure and managed energy transition.
“Energy policy cannot be made in Westminster alone without listening to the people and communities who have powered this country for the last 50 years.
text:
An early visit by Prime Minister Andy Burnham to meet North Sea energy operators and their workforce could mark a crucial turning point in government attitudes towards home-grown energy and the future of the offshore industry, says David Whitehouse, Chief Executive of Offshore Energies UK (OEUK).

OEUK has requested an urgent prime ministerial visit to operators in Scotland and supply-chains in the Northeast of England, arguing that energy production must be incentivised ahead of increasing reliance on imported oil and gas.

Energy policy cannot be made in Westminster alone.

The new government has an opportunity to reset the relationship with the North Sea industry and the communities that depend on it. The choice is not between oil and gas or clean energy. It is whether we produce the energy we need here in the UK, with our own workers and supply chains, or import more from overseas at higher cost and with higher emissions.

Using imported liquified natural gas (LNG) from America or Qatar which is increasingly being used to replace North Sea gas, involves carbon emissions that are four times higher.

OEUK analysis shows that a reset addressing reform of the regulatory and tax framework for the North Sea industry, including early implementation of the government’s proposed Oil and Gas Price Mechanism, could unlock an additional £50 billion in oil and gas investment.

Over the next decade alone this would increase capital investment by £26 billion, boost tax receipts by more than £13 billion and support tens of thousands of jobs.

It would also help the UK meet at least half of its oil and gas needs from domestic production between now and 2050.

Faster reform could also cut the imported liquified natural gas (LNG) share of UK gas supplies to 6% by 2035, compared with 46% without reform.

Independent polling data from Opinium earlier this month shows that the government’s own supporters are looking for a reset on energy policy from the new prime minister. Labour voters favour scrapping the ban on exploration and following Norway’s pragmatic approach to new licences by 42% to 35%. And almost 70% of Labour voters say the UK should prioritise North Sea oil and gas production compared to just 9% who said it doesn’t matter where oil and gas comes from.

David Whitehouse chief executive of Offshore Energies UK said:

“The UK will still need oil and gas for decades to come. The question is whether we produce as much of that energy as possible here — supporting our own jobs, communities and economy — or rely increasingly on imports while exporting investment and economic value overseas. Government policy should back North Sea production as part of a secure and managed energy transition.

“Energy policy cannot be made in Westminster alone without listening to the people and communities who have powered this country for the last 50 years. For too long, offshore workers, engineers, technicians and those across the energy supply chain have been talked about rather than listened to. A visit to meet the North Sea workforce would demonstrate that the new Government intends to build a different relationship with the people and communities at the heart of Britain’s energy system.

The new Prime Minister must now turn listening into action. Words of support for projects such as Jackdaw and Rosebank cannot be a substitute for the policy reset our country needs. The new Government must back North Sea oil and gas over increased reliance on imports — delivering the fiscal and regulatory reforms required to unlock investment, protect domestic jobs, strengthen energy security and support the energy transition.”

title: Germany to limit new renewable support in bid to ease grid pressure, lower costs
description:
In a bid to lower energy transition costs, the government wants to cut support for small-scale rooftop solar, and lower compensation for forced curtailments of larger renewables projects in case of grid overload.
Germany must overhaul its renewable energy support scheme under the Renewable Energy Act (EEG) before the current funding regime expires at the end of 2026, partly to comply with new EU state aid rules requiring windfall-profit clawbacks from 2027.
“We see the current drafts as a significant setback for renewable energy,” said BEE head Ursula Heinen-Esser.
New renewable projects in areas with grid bottlenecks will only receive an automatic grid connection if they agree to forgo curtailment compensation payments.
From 2027 onwards, small rooftop solar installations will continue to receive a feed-in tariff for their first three years, albeit at a lower rate than current support.
text:
Germany’s government has tabled its proposal for reducing incentives for new solar and wind energy projects in areas with a congested electricity network, and asked industry groups and federal states for feedback. In a bid to lower energy transition costs, the government wants to cut support for small-scale rooftop solar, and lower compensation for forced curtailments of larger renewables projects in case of grid overload.

Germany must overhaul its renewable energy support scheme under the Renewable Energy Act (EEG) before the current funding regime expires at the end of 2026, partly to comply with new EU state aid rules requiring windfall-profit clawbacks from 2027. Priority grid access for renewables, which guarantee developers both connection and remuneration, has long been a cornerstone of Germany's energy transition, but grid expansion has lagged far behind renewables additions.

The renewable energy association (BEE) and the solar industry association (BSW-Solar) both heavily criticised the reforms to the renewable energy act (EEG) and the grid connection package, saying the proposals jeopardised investments worth billions and put tens of thousands of jobs at risk. “We see the current drafts as a significant setback for renewable energy,” said BEE head Ursula Heinen-Esser.

The reforms sent to associations for feedback were watered down compared to initial proposals. New renewable projects in areas with grid bottlenecks will only receive an automatic grid connection if they agree to forgo curtailment compensation payments. However, the threshold was raised and will apply to areas where five percent of the previous year’s electricity could not be fed into the grid, up from three percent. The period to forgo remuneration payments during times in which produced electricity could not be fed into the grid was also shortened from ten to six years. Moreover, the volume of uncompensated curtailed electricity will be capped at between 10 and 20 percent of annual production.

From 2027 onwards, small rooftop solar installations will continue to receive a feed-in tariff for their first three years, albeit at a lower rate than current support. Owners currently receive a fixed feed-in tariff. Initial plans had foreseen a complete scrap of guaranteed remuneration. Under current plans, transitional payments would be phased out completely by 2030.

Associations were given three working days to submit comments, a timeline they called “unacceptable”, “inadequate” and “inappropriate”, adding that legislation with such far-reaching consequences should be subject to careful scrutiny.

Both reforms were under government negotiations for months. They form part of the economy ministry’s push to make the energy transition more cost-efficient and align renewable expansion with grid capacity. Economy minister Katherina Reiche, a member of chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservatives (CDU), argued that renewable projects should bear the financial risk in case their electricity needed to be curtailed, and that small solar panels had already reached market maturity and needed no support. The renewables industry agrees that Germany can increase the transition’s efficiency, but points out that proposals are likely to slow down the expansion of wind and solar power.

Germany aims to cover 80 percent of its electricity consumption with renewable sources by 2030. The cabinet is set to agree on the reforms on 29 July.

title: 2027 Chevy Bolt is a critical darling with a looming expiration date - Detroit Free Press
description:
Bolt sales may be strong for today’s market, but may not come close to what the old Bolt was able to pull, according to Kelley Blue Book.
Car and Driver magazine named the 2027 Chevrolet Bolt the 2026 EV of the Year for its low price and high performance.
But that level of popularity won't save the subcompact electric vehicle.
“They’re not going to come anywhere close to sales of the old Bolt,” Tucker said.
Moving faster and saving costs when it comes to electric vehicle production is vital, Tucker said.
text:
Car and Driver raved that the Bolt offers the range, charging capability, available technology, and practicality that will make it easy for buyers to make the switch to EV.

Bolt sales may be strong for today’s market, but may not come close to what the old Bolt was able to pull, according to Kelley Blue Book.

Production of the Bolt at General Motors’ Fairfax Assembly Plant in Kansas will be replaced when the gas-powered Equinox starts in 2027 and the next generation Buick Envision in 2028.

Car and Driver magazine named the 2027 Chevrolet Bolt the 2026 EV of the Year for its low price and high performance.

But that level of popularity won't save the subcompact electric vehicle.

Despite the upgrades from past models and rave reviews, the car is still planned for a limited run, which will last 18 months at General Motors’ Fairfax Assembly Plant in Kansas before it is replaced by production of the gas-powered Equinox starting in 2027 and the next generation Buick Envision it currently makes in China in 2028.

Chevy’s petite and popular EV returned to market this year with a cost-effective lithium-iron phosphate battery and $30,000 price point.

Upgraded batteries, software and motors bring the vehicle up to date with GM’s newer EVs like the GMC Hummer, Chevrolet Blazer EV and Cadillac Lyriq, and rely on GM’s proprietary Ultium propulsion system. The Bolt uses the same motor as the Chevrolet Equinox with an output of 210 horsepower.

Tony Quiroga, editor in chief of Car and Driver, said in a statement the Bolt’s value placed it ahead of its peers.

“For $28,995 the Bolt offers the range, charging capability, available technology, and practicality that will make it easy for buyers to make the switch from gas to EV,” Quiroga said. “It makes us smile because it’s fun to drive and provides the deep satisfaction of getting more car than you paid for.”

Strong sales amid EV slowdown

In the second quarter, GM sold 3,433 Chevrolet Bolts, up from 791 it sold in the first quarter when production began. Those figures may be strong for today’s market, but may not come close to what the old Bolt was able to pull, according to Sean Tucker, managing editor of Kelly Blue Book, which is owned by Cox Automotive.

Bolt sales average between 1,400 and 1,600 per month, according to Kelley Blue Book, which is pretty good for a market without federal tax incentives. The Bolt either leads sales for the segment or comes in second, trading places back and forth with the new Toyota CHR. Sales are well above the Nissan Leaf, which Tucker considers more natural competition for the Bolt.

But low volumes may be a new normal for the segment. Tucker said if the current sales trends continue, Bolt sales would likely reach just 28,800 vehicles sold within the planned 18 months of production.

In 2022, sales reached 64,322 vehicles, for smaller Bolts and EUVs.

“They’re not going to come anywhere close to sales of the old Bolt,” Tucker said. “But I think demand for a subcompact electric vehicle is relatively low right now.”

The average transaction cost for the Bolt from January through June 2026 was $31,006, according to Kelley Blue Book data. The average days in dealership inventory in the second quarter was 54.6 days.

So why cancel the vehicle?

Sam Abuelsamid, vice president of market research at Telemetry, called the decision “stupid.”

“Why even bother to build it again if you’re only going to do it for 18 months? It makes no sense. For all the reengineering work. It’s stupid,” he said. “It’s reasonably roomy. It’s affordable. Consumers will maybe see the benefit of a car like this if interest rates stay high. This can keep the monthly payments down.”

Another huge bonus for the Bolt is its the only vehicle priced around $30,000 built in the United States, Abuelsamid said. Many similarly priced vehicles like the Chevrolet Trax and Buick Envista are built in South Korea. If GM were to continue building this vehicle it would reinforce its commitment to affordable electrification and affordable American-made vehicles.

Why the Bolt stands out

Meanwhile, part of what distinguishes the Bolt launch is the approach GM has taken to building it.

Fairfax Assembly, the first GM factory in North America to use this strategy, builds Bolts in batches of 30 of the same color and trim level. That uniformity allows for more consistency and fewer errors as the company worked to quickly scale short-term production.

“But I don’t think this car is about sales for GM,” Tucker said. “They’re using it to experiment with new methods of building.”

In a typical car factory, he said, cars coming down the line may be one make but with different content, for example a green Bolt with an eight-speaker stereo may be followed by a blue Bolt with a 12-speaker stereo followed by a red Bolt with eight-speaker stereo again. By reducing the number of times line workers need to switch out parts and double check the content of a model heading down the line, it could reduce errors and allow the line to move faster.

Moving faster and saving costs when it comes to electric vehicle production is vital, Tucker said. According to the International Energy Agency, about one in four cars sold globally is electric. In the United States, it’s closer to 6%.

”How do you compete in both markets? You have to get good at electric cars, you have to remain good at non-electric cars,” Tucker said. “Right now, it’s about what they can learn from (the Bolt).”

But even as a dry run for future EVs, the Bolt still has fans.

Car and Driver's 2026 EV of the Year ballot had 25 of the newest electric car models from 14 different automakers, according to the magazine. The Bolt won out against competitors Audi A6 e-tron, Cadillac Escalade IQL, Cadillac Optiq, Dodge Charger Daytona 4-Door, GMC Sierra EV, Lexus ES350e, Lexus ES500e, Lexus RZ550e, Lucid Gravity Touring, Mercedes-Benz CLA250+, Nissan Leaf, Polestar 4, Porsche Macan GTS Electric, Subaru Solterra, Subaru Trailseeker, Subaru Uncharted, Tesla Model 3, Tesla Model Y, Tesla Model Y Performance, Toyota bZ, Toyota bZ Woodland, and Toyota C-HR.

“The '27 Bolt's comprehensive glow-up couldn’t come at a better time. America doesn't need another hyper-powered, hyper-expensive EV. This Chevy does something no other EV in our market has before: It democratizes modern battery-electric powertrain technology at a sub-$30K price while also offering the core creature comforts modern consumers expect,” Car and Driver surmised. “The fact that Chevy pins a $28,995 price to an EV with a spacious and versatile cabin, solid real-world driving range, spirited dynamics, and a general ease of use makes the '27 Bolt the right EV for right now.”

Jackie Charniga covers General Motors for the Free Press. Reach her at jcharniga@freepress.com.

title: BasiGo Partners with Rubis Energy Kenya to Expand Fast-Charging Infrastructure
description:
BasiGo has announced a new partnership with energy solutions provider Rubis Energy Kenya to expand fast-charging infrastructure along the country’s key transport corridors.
Open to the public; the stations will be used to provide access to charging infrastructure for electric buses, vans, trucks, passenger vehicles and more.
Jit Bhattacharya, CEO and Co-Founder of BasiGo, said: Scaling electric mobility requires infrastructure, and that’s exactly what this partnership with Rubis is building.
We are creating the infrastructure that will power EV operations beyond Nairobi and connect communities across Kenya.
This is a massive step forward for Kenya’s E-mobility industry, and it is a model we intend to replicate as we scale across the region.
text:
BasiGo has announced a new partnership with energy solutions provider Rubis Energy Kenya to expand fast-charging infrastructure along the country’s key transport corridors.

The move is expected to enable the growth of electric mobility across the country, with the first charging station opened under the partnership now fully operational at the Rubis service station in Sabaki, Athi River, with additional sites in Meru, Nanyuki, and Nyeri scheduled to commissioned later this month.

Open to the public; the stations will be used to provide access to charging infrastructure for electric buses, vans, trucks, passenger vehicles and more.

Equipped with both CCS2 and GB/T DC 100kW fast chargers, the Sabaki charging station aims to provide charge for a typical passenger vehicle in under an hour, with compatibility extending across a wide range of commercial electric vehicles.

All sites under the partnership will feature similar charging technology, and offer charging at an indicative rate of KES 48 per kWh, ensuring consistent and reliable experience across the network.

Jit Bhattacharya, CEO and Co-Founder of BasiGo, said:

Scaling electric mobility requires infrastructure, and that’s exactly what this partnership with Rubis is building. We are creating the infrastructure that will power EV operations beyond Nairobi and connect communities across Kenya.

This is a massive step forward for Kenya’s E-mobility industry, and it is a model we intend to replicate as we scale across the region.
